drills.title: vs Mohamed_Behery (840) — Queens Pawn Opening Horwitz Defense
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here — up more than six pawns of advantage — and the position was begging for Nd5+. Your knight jumping into d5 forks the king on e7 and rips the center open: after exd5, Rfe1+ kicks the king to d6, and Qxf8+ just wins the rook on f8 outright. Instead you grabbed the pawn on h7, which feels natural but ignores that exposed king on e7. Black gets Rd8 and Qf6+ with real counterplay, and you end up giving material back with gxf4. When the enemy king is stuck in the center, look for checks that drag it further out before you go pawn-hunting.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: You had mate in two on the board. Nf4+ forces the king to e3 — its only legal square — and then Bc5 is checkmate, your dark-squared bishop covering everything with no escape. Instead you grabbed the pawn on e5 with check, which feels forcing but lets White block with Ne4. After Bxe4 the king wriggles out, and White even gets to play Qc1 and castle long. You went from a forced mate to just a big material edge — still winning, but you handed back the cleanest possible finish. When you're up huge and see a check, ask if it's the one that ends the game, not just the one that wins a pawn.

drills.coachNote: Your queen on g3 had a forcing sequence sitting right there: Qg3+ drives the king to e2, its only square, then Qxe5+ grabs a pawn with another check, and after Kf2 Qd4+ Ke2 you keep the king pinned down while picking up material. Instead you played the quiet Ne6, developing the knight but handing back the initiative. White gets to tuck the queen away with Qc1, and while you still find Qxe5+ later, you've let the king breathe and lost some of your bite. When the enemy king is exposed and a check is on the board, take it before you develop — every tempo you give back is one the king uses to hide.

drills.coachNote: Look at the pawn on d4 — the queen on d1 'defends' it down the file, but White's own bishop on d3 sits right between them, blocking that defense completely. So d4 is actually hanging, and Nxd4 just wins it clean. Instead you took the knight on e5, which looks like the same idea, but that knight is protected by the f4 pawn, so Nxe5 fxe5 is just an even trade — you got nothing extra for it. Before you capture, check who's actually defending each piece, not just who's standing near it, because a blocked defender doesn't count as a defender at all.

Playing d4 pushes a queenside pawn while ignoring all of it, and White pounces with Be6+, forcing Kh8, then Qg6 lines straight up on that hole with real mating threats while Be4 keeps piling on. What you needed was Qg5, bringing the queen back to defend and trade off attackers — after Be6+ Kh8 f4 Qg3+ Qf2 you force queens off and the danger evaporates. When your king has an airhole like that, defense comes before pushing pawns elsewhere.

drills.coachNote: This is the one that cost you the game, so let's really look at it. Black's knight on e3 isn't just annoying — it's guarding the g2 square, and Black's queen is already sitting on g4 aiming right at it. That means Qxg2 is already checkmate: your king can't recapture because the knight backs it up, and nothing else defends g2. You had to remove that knight immediately with fxe3, which also opens the position fine for you — after fxe3 Qf5 Nh4 Qxf7 Rxf7 Rxf7 you're doing well. Instead Qe2 developed a piece while the mate sat right there, and Black simply played Qxg2#. Whenever an enemy piece is camped next to your king, check what square it's covering before you do anything else.

drills.title: vs nodfri (676) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, just mopping up — and Re3 pulls your rook off the back rank at the worst moment. The instant e8 is empty, White has Bd5+, a check down the a2-g8 diagonal your rook was blocking, and after Kf8, Rc8+ shoves you right back to e8 anyway just to survive. You've burned two tempi and let White's rook and bishop swarm your king, turning a crushing position shaky. Simple Rf8 kept the back rank solid and let you take the dangerous f6 pawn next move. White's knight takes it, Nxe4, you recapture Nxe4, and then the rook on e1 swoops in with Rxe4 and wins the piece back a second time, because your rook still can't see through your own bishop. You've traded a bishop and a knight for a single knight — a piece down for nothing. Be6 was the safe square: it offers a clean trade, Bxe6 fxe6, with no hidden defenders to miscount.

drills.title: vs Twister21checkersChess (676) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: You were up so much here it was basically decided, but Bd6 hands some of it back. Your bishop on e5 was already dominating that diagonal; moving it to d6 lets Black's rook swing to b6 with real activity, and your queen has to shuffle to a4 just to stay coordinated. You still won, but you gave back nearly 15 pawns of advantage for nothing. Rd7 was the clean finish — drop the rook onto the seventh rank while the bishop still guards d6 from e5, so if Black tries Rd6, Bxd6 just wins the exchange outright. When you're crushing like this, a rook on the seventh kills counterplay faster than moving a piece that's already doing its job.

You get there in the end, but you let Black generate free activity for no reason, the kind of thing that turns a clean technical win into a stressful one. Kf7 was the fix — it doesn't stop the pawn, but it clears e8 so that after bxa8=Q, your other rook on f8 can fly down the now-open eighth rank and take the new queen right back with Rxa8. Same promotion either way; the difference is whether you get it back or just hand it over.

Be7 sidesteps the whole issue — same development, safer square — and if White still plays d5, it only hits the knight, which hops back to b8 and reroutes to d7. In the opening, always ask what a pawn push can attack before you plant a piece on its path.

Rf7+ was the way to keep fighting: check the black king first instead of shuffling your own king, drive it back with Rf7+ Kg2, then swing the rook to e7 and even win the e3 pawn. When you're behind on material, look for the rook move that invades and grabs pawns, not the one that just looks tidy.

drills.explanation: Qf8 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Nd5 ran into Qd6+, costing about 5.5 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs EddsSalinas (516) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: The real danger is White's knight on f7 — it forks your queen on d8 and rook on h8 at once, and that's the threat to answer, not develop around. Nd5 ignores it, so White cashes in with Qd6+ first: your king on d7 must go to e8, then Qxd8+ just wins the queen outright, since that same knight on f7 defends d8 and you can't recapture — Kxf7 only comes after the queen's already gone. Qf8 solves it directly: the queen steps off d8 and covers h8 along the back rank in one move, so even after Nxh8 Qxh8 c4 Ke7 h5 you're down the exchange but stable, and your king reaches e7 instead of getting hunted. When two pieces sit on one knight's fork squares, that's the only thing worth calculating.

drills.explanation: O-O was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Bd6 left that piece hanging: after Nxd6+ it's simply lost.
drills.title: vs EddsSalinas (516) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on b4 was safe there — the problem is that d6 is undefended (your c6 pawn covers b5 and d5, not d6), and White's knight on e4 is one hop from landing on it. Bd6 walks straight onto that square: Nxd6+ wins the bishop for free, and because your king's still on e8 it comes with check, so after Ke7 the knight jumps again to f7, forking your queen on d8 — the same knight-fork pattern that costs you again later in this game. O-O sidesteps it entirely by getting your king off the e-file first; even if White grabs the bishop with cxb4 anyway, you get real play with Nxe4 Qxe4 Nf6, hitting the queen. Castle before relocating other pieces — an uncastled king turns ordinary tactics into forcing ones.

drills.explanation: Bg7+ forks the king on h8 and the king on h8 — one of them falls next move. In the game, Qxb7 ran into Qxh6, costing about 6.2 pawns of advantage.
drills.opening: Indian Game East Indian London System
drills.title: vs Moksha212 (842) — Indian Game East Indian London System
drills.coachNote: You had Bg7+ sitting right there, and it wins material outright: check the king on h8, the only legal reply is Rxg7, and that rook was the defender of c8 — so Qxc8+ picks it off next with check. Instead Qxb7 just grabs a pawn, and that let the tactic vanish: Black's queen on h4 was free to swoop in with Qxh6 and win your bishop straight back, turning a +5.2 position into a real fight. Bg7+ is a deflection — force the defender off c8, then take what it left behind. Before cashing in a free pawn, always check whether a forcing move gets you something bigger first.

drills.explanation: Bh2 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Bg5 left that piece hanging: after Nxg5 it's simply lost.
drills.opening: Indian Game East Indian London System
drills.title: vs Moksha212 (842) — Indian Game East Indian London System
drills.coachNote: Before moving that bishop, notice what Black's knight on e4 already covers — g5, f6, d6, c5 among others; it's deep in your position and anything you send to those squares just hangs. Bg5 does exactly that: Nxg5 wins the bishop clean, and even after your Nxg5 recaptures, Black's queen on d8 was sitting on the wide-open d8-g5 diagonal the whole time, so Qxg5 mops up your knight too — you're down a full piece for nothing. Bh2 tucks the bishop off that diagonal and keeps developing normally; after Nc5 Be2 e4 Nd4 Ne5 the position stays level and nothing's hanging. Whenever an enemy knight sits deep in your camp, map every square it touches before deciding where your own pieces go.

drills.explanation: g4 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Rxc7 ran into Rec8, costing about 3.1 pawns of advantage.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs Zaratustra25 (819) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're already down the exchange, so the priority is keeping pieces on, not simplifying — Rxc7 does the opposite. Grab that pawn and Black answers Rec8, attacking your rook on c7 and forcing Rxc8+ Rxc8: rooks come off, and now it's just your lone knight on c6 against a full rook, a much harder position to hold than a move ago. g4 keeps the tension instead, grabbing kingside space without inviting a trade, so after Rac8 Rd5 Re6 Rc5 Ke8 your rook stays active with real chances to cause problems. When you're down material, don't let a free pawn talk you into the trade that simplifies toward the ending your opponent wants.

drills.explanation: Ra1 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Nc6 ran into Bxd1, costing about 2.7 pawns of advantage.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs Zaratustra25 (819) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Before Nc6, look at the diagonal from g4 to d1 — your rook on d1 sits completely undefended on it, with only empty squares on f3 and e2 in between. Moving your knight to c6 does nothing about that, so Black just plays Bxd1, and after Rxd1 you've dropped the exchange for nothing, turning a roughly level position sharply in Black's favor. Ra1 was the fix: it simply steps the rook off that diagonal to safety, after which you're free to expand with a4 and Rfc8 and press on the queenside. The habit to build: scan every open diagonal aimed at your own pieces, not just the ones aimed at your king.

drills.explanation: h6 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Re1+ left that piece hanging: after Rxe1 it's simply lost.
drills.title: vs jordyjumps (611) — Van t Kruijs Opening
drills.coachNote: The real problem on this board is the queen on c7, sitting deep in your position — not anything about trading rooks. Re1+ just invites Rxe1, and once that trade happens White's other rook swings to e2 with Rce2, doubling up exactly where you needed defenders, while your queen alone on f3 can't hold off a queen and two rooks. You were actually better here before this move, and that's what got thrown away. h6 first gives your king breathing room and keeps both rooks on the board to meet Qc7 with numbers, instead of handing White a simplifying trade that helps the stronger attacker.

drills.explanation: e4 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, f6 ran into c4, costing about 1.7 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs jordyjumps (611) — Van t Kruijs Opening
drills.coachNote: Your knight on d7 wants to land on f6 — that's the whole point of the engine's own line, Ndf6, hitting d4 and getting you developed fast. Playing the pawn to f6 instead slams that door shut yourself, and White gets to strike your center with c4; after Bb4+ Nbc3 Ne7 you're just rearranging pieces with nothing to show for it. e4 was the move — it grabs space, jams White's bishop on b2 against your own pawn chain, and keeps f6 open for the knight to use properly. Push pawns to open lanes for your pieces, not to lock them out of the game.

drills.explanation: Rd7 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Ra7 ran into Rxg4+, costing about 10.3 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs CeliaDuchesne (819) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Two things needed your attention and Ra7 handled neither. Your bishop on g4 sits on the same rank as Black's rook on f4, so it's hanging to Rxg4+, and Black's pawn on d2 is one step from queening. Chasing the a6 pawn ignores both — Rxg4+ forces Kh2, then d1=Q, and your bishop is gone while Black has a brand-new queen, turning a crushing position into a scramble. Rd7 solves it at the root: your rook is already on the d-file, so even after Rxg4+ Kh2 d1=Q you just play Rxd1 and pocket the new queen immediately. When you're way ahead, find your opponent's one resource first, before grabbing more material.

drills.explanation: Rad1 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Re2 ran into Nf3+, costing about 3.5 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs CeliaDuchesne (819) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's knight on e5 had one shot you needed to spot first: Nf3+ forks your king on g1 and your queen on h4 in one move. Re2 put your rook on a square defended only by your knight on d2, so once Nf3+ forces Nxf3 to save the queen, that knight leaves e2 undefended and Rxe2 wins your rook for free. Rad1 sidesteps it entirely — it brings the other rook into play without ever touching e1, so the same fork has nothing to win. Before you move a piece off a square, check what it was quietly guarding — here, that rook on e2 was standing on a landmine.

drills.explanation: bxc6 simply wins the bishop on c6 — it wasn't adequately defended. In the game, Bd7 left that piece hanging: after Bxd7+ it's simply lost.
drills.title: vs Dgreek46 (678) — Caro Kann Defense
drills.coachNote: That bishop on c6 giving you check is just hanging — nothing white recaptures if you take it with bxc6. Instead Bd7 blocks the check, which only trades bishop for bishop after Bxd7+ Qxd7, when bxc6 wins the piece outright and leaves you a full bishop ahead instead of dead level. Blocking a check with a piece is a fine instinct, but always check first whether you can simply capture the checking piece instead — b7 was sitting right there ready to do it for free. That one question, capture before block, is what swings this game from roughly equal to completely winning.

drills.explanation: Qxd4+ forks the king on g1 and the king on g1 — one of them falls next move. In the game, Nxd2 left that piece hanging: after Qxd2 it's simply lost.
drills.title: vs Dgreek46 (678) — Caro Kann Defense
drills.coachNote: You were already crushing, up around six and a half pawns, but notice the order available to you: Qxd4+ grabs a free pawn and checks the king, forcing Kh1 before you even touch the bishop on d2. You played Nxd2 straight away instead, and White simply replies Qxd2 — an even trade, but you left the d4 pawn on the board and gave up the free tempo that check would have bought. Even in a totally won position, look for the forcing move first — checks and captures with tempo before the quiet ones — so you collect everything on offer instead of leaving pawns behind.

drills.explanation: Qc7# is checkmate on the spot — the king has no escape squares. In the game, Qb7+ ran into Kd8, costing about 9.2 pawns of advantage.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs aksu10ten (599) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Look at the king on c8 — Qc7 right now is mate, your queen covers every square he could run to. Qb7+ is check too, but it only pushes him to d8, so instead of ending the game on the spot you're chasing him across the board, and Black even claws back a check with Qxg4+ before you finally wrap it up. You still won on the huge material edge, but that's a nine-pawn swing in engine terms between game over immediately and just should be fine eventually. Whenever a check is on the board, spend one extra second asking whether the king actually has a square left — if he doesn't, that's your move.

drills.explanation: Qd7 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Qd3 ran into f5, costing about 7.8 pawns of advantage.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs aksu10ten (599) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You had a completely winning position, and Qd7 was the move that ends it cleanly - it dives behind Black's lines, hits c7, and even Black's desperation try Qxf2+ Rxf2 e5 just loses the rook on h7 to Qxh7. Qd3 instead sits passively and hands Black the initiative: f5! rips the kingside open, and after gxf5 e6! fxe6 your king on g1 is suddenly exposed to the queen on f3 and rook on h7, with your bishop still dead on h2. You gave back most of a completely winning advantage for nothing. When you're up huge, keep hunting - don't retreat and let the opponent generate counterplay.

drills.explanation: Rd1 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Re5 ran into Qxc1+, costing about 3.1 pawns of advantage.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs Sadrios (652) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Before you even think about activating a rook, scan for what's hanging - and your rook on c1 was sitting undefended right on the a3-c1 diagonal that Black's queen already owns. Re5 does nothing about that, so Black just plays Qxc1+, and after Kh2 you're down a full rook while Black keeps rolling with Rg6, eyeing your queen on g3. Rd1 was the fix: it simply steps the rook off that diagonal, and the position stays a fight rather than a lost cause. This one's a reminder that 'the most active move' isn't the same question as 'is anything of mine hanging right now' - always answer the second one first.

drills.explanation: c4 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, dxe5 left that piece hanging: after Nxe5 it's simply lost.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs Sadrios (652) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Look at Black's queen on d5 and the advanced pawn on e4 sitting in front of it - c4 hits the queen first, and once it steps back the e4 pawn loses its defender, so you simply win it with Nxe4. That's the move the position wanted. dxe5 throws that away: it releases the central tension for nothing, Black recaptures with Nxe5 landing a knight beautifully in the center, and when you chase it with c4 anyway, Black has Nxc4! snatching your pawn and untangling before you can cash in on e4. You turned a comfortable structural edge into an equal position. Keep central tension alive when there's a move that wins material outright instead of releasing it automatically.

drills.explanation: Qd2 forks the rook on e1 and the knight on h6 — one of them falls next move. In the game, Qb6 ran into Nxf7+, costing about 3.2 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Ntk2711 (850) — Caro Kann Defense Karpov Variation
drills.coachNote: That knight on h6 has been eyeing f7 the whole time, defended by White's bishop on c4 along the c4-f7 diagonal, so Nxf7+ forking your king on h8 is a live threat. Qb6 ignores it completely: Nxf7+ Kg7 and White's rook swings over with Rf3, opening a highway toward your king, with Qg6 piling on. Qd2 was right there instead - it grabs the c2 pawn and keeps your own attack going, and even after Ng4 Qxc2 Bxf7 Bxb3 you're mopping up material safely. This is the same f7 fork you had to dodge two moves ago - a piece aiming at a square doesn't stop aiming just because your attention moved elsewhere.

drills.explanation: Qh5 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Qd4 ran into Nxf7+, costing about 1.4 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Ntk2711 (850) — Caro Kann Defense Karpov Variation
drills.coachNote: That knight on h6 is already lined up for Nxf7+, forking your king on h8, and Qd4 does nothing about it. Play it out: Nxf7+ forces Rxf7, and then Rxf7! wins the exchange outright - White's rook takes your rook, netting a full rook for a knight. Qh5 keeps you safe and active instead, staying on the kingside where lines like Nf5 c4 Ng3 Qh6 show you continuing to press while the knight on h6 never gets a clean shot at f7. Whenever a piece is one hop from forking your king, that has to be answered before anything else - even a natural-looking centralizing move like Qd4.

drills.explanation: a5 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Ng6 left that piece hanging: after Nxg6 it's simply lost.
drills.title: vs FlokieXIV (796) — Caro Kann Defense Advance Variation
drills.coachNote: Your knight on e7 heading to g6 walks right into White's knight on h4, which already covers that square - so Nxg6 fxg6 is basically forced. It's only a piece trade, but look what it costs: your f7 pawn disappears, you're left with doubled g-pawns, the f-file opens in front of your own king, and White follows with a5, shoving your bishop off b6 to the passive c7 square. That's your structure wrecked for nothing. a5 fit the actual plan instead - grabbing queenside space, with lines like b5 c5 Ndf3 Qc7 keeping your position healthy and flexible. Before you jump a knight to a square, check who else is already aiming at it.

drills.explanation: Ne5 keeps the attack on the stranded king on f6 alive: the threat is Nd7+, and after Qg8, Nd7+ Kg5 h4+ drags the king even further up the board while your queen sits on h7. Qxb7 won a bishop but allowed Qd5 — a queen trade you can't decline (Qxd5 exd5) — and with queens off, the attack on f6 vanished, about five pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs sudharsanee (850) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Variation
drills.coachNote: Black's king is stranded out on f6, and that's the real story of the position - the winning plan is to keep hunting it, not stop for material. Ne5 does exactly that: after Qg8 Nd7+ you're checking the king again, and h4+ Nxh4 shows it still getting chased. Qxb7 grabs the bishop but lets Black hit back with Qd5!, offering a queen trade you can't dodge - Qxd5 exd5 Nd2 and the mating attack evaporates into a technical endgame you now have to convert the hard way. You gave back more than five pawns of advantage by taking the 'free' piece instead of the move that kept the king running. When the enemy king is this exposed, chasing it beats grabbing material almost every time.

drills.explanation: Ne5 puts the knight on a square the d4 pawn protects and attacks the knight on g6. If Nxe5, dxe5+ regains the piece with check, and after Qxe5 your Qf3+ keeps queens on against his airy king. Your Qf3+ instead offered the trade Black wanted: Qxf3 gxf3 killed all the pressure, and Nf4 came next, poking at the h3 pawn.
drills.title: vs sudharsanee (850) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Variation
drills.coachNote: Same pattern as a few moves back - Black's king is still stuck on f6, and Ne5 keeps the hunt alive: after Nxe5 dxe5+ you recapture with check, and only then does Qf3+ really bite, hitting Kg7 with the king shoved back further. Playing Qf3+ right away instead invites Qxf3, and after gxf3 your kingside pawns end up doubled on the f-file while Black's knight jumps into f4 with real activity. You still keep a good chunk of the edge, but you swapped hunting the king for a queen trade and a messier structure while it was still out in the open. Insert the forcing move that gains tempo - a check, a fork - before reaching for the trade that simplifies everything.

drills.explanation: Both your queen and rook could capture the knight on f4, but Qxf4 is the right way: it wins the knight while the rook on f8 keeps guarding its partner on e8. Rxf4 abandoned that rook — Qxe8+ snapped it off with check, and after Kh7, Qe6 left White completely consolidated. Taking with the wrong piece cost about six pawns.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Look at your rook on f8 before grabbing that knight — it's the only piece guarding e8. Play Rxf4 and e8 is suddenly undefended, so White fires Qxe8+, picking off your rook with check on king g8 for nothing more than the knight you'd just won. You're up a piece for an instant, then down a rook for a knight, and after Kh7 Qe6 White's queen is dominating d6 and e4 too. Qxf4 takes the same knight with your queen instead, so f8 never moves and e8 stays covered — you keep pushing with ...e3, opening lines instead of losing material. Before any capture, ask what the moving piece was protecting.

drills.explanation: a6 strikes at White's overextended queenside: after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook enters the game down the a-file, and b5 is met calmly by Ra8. Castling let White play Qe2, hitting your knight on c4 — a piece with no defenders — and you had to scramble with c6 and b5 just to hold it, leaving White a wedge pawn on c6.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Before tucking your king away, look at your knight on c4 — it sits on the same diagonal as e2, and nothing of yours defends it. Castling ignores that, so White plays Qe2 and the knight's attacked with no safe square; you scramble with ...c6, White answers bxc6, and even after ...b5 you still haven't solved the real problem and you're worse for it. a6 deals with that side of the board directly — it hits the b5 pawn, and after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook lands on an open file while the knight on c4 finally has support coming. Fix your loose pieces before you spend a move on castling.

drills.explanation: You were a full piece up and just needed to consolidate. c5 gains space, and the knight calmly reroutes to c6 next with b6 and normal development to follow. Ng4 put the knight on a square covered by White's queen all the way back on d1 — Qxg4 took it for nothing, handing the extra piece straight back.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Before you send a knight to g4, check who's watching that square — White's queen sits on d1, and d1-e2-f3-g4 is a wide-open diagonal, so Ng4 just hands the knight over for nothing with Qxg4. There's no trick coming back for it; you're simply down a full piece from that move onward. c5 was the real move — it grabs queenside space, prepares ...Nc6 and ...b6, and keeps your development, including Bb2 ideas, intact. Every time you send a piece deep, trace the files and diagonals into that square first: if a queen or rook already has a clear look at it, it isn't a jump, it's a gift.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on e6 and White's bishop on a2 are staring at each other down the same long diagonal — that trade is coming no matter what, so take it on your terms with Bxa2. After Rxa2 you swing a rook to e8 and then e6, active and still winning big. Play the quieter Rad8 instead and White gets to dictate terms: Bh6 pokes at g7, forcing ...g6, and then Bxe6 fxe6 trades the same pair of bishops anyway — except now your kingside pawns are loosened for nothing. You were already up a mountain of material here, so the lesson is efficiency: take the trade that's coming before you get shuffled into a worse version of it.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your knight on c5 has a shot at c6 — Nxc6 forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8 in one move. Even if Black tries to wriggle free with ...Qd6, you just take the rook anyway with Nxd8, winning a full rook for the knight and mopping up ...Qxg5 besides. a4 skips right past that and shuffles a queenside pawn instead, so Black gets to play ...Nxe5, trade off your strong knight, and plant a piece on e4 — most of your 4.8 pawn cushion evaporates for nothing. When one of your pieces is eyeing two enemy pieces at once, that's the move to look for before anything quieter.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: That same fork was still there — Nxc6 still wins material by hitting the queen on e7 and the rook on d8 — but now there's a second reason to look at it: your knight on e5 is only 'defended' by the queen on e3 through the e-file, and Black's own knight on e4 sits right in that line, blocking the defense completely. b5 addresses neither point, so Black simply plays ...Nxe5 and picks up a full knight for free. You try to generate something back with bxa6, bxa6, and Nb3, but none of it buys back the piece. When a piece looks defended, check that the line to it is actually open.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: There was a forced mate sitting on the board: Rxf7 grabs the pawn, and after ...Re2, it's Rg7+ Kh8 Rg8# — your rook on e7 and bishop on f6 already had his king boxed in on the back rank with nowhere to run. Qg5 throws that away entirely, and instead of finishing the game you let Black play ...Rxf2, snatching a pawn right next to your own king and forcing you to spend moves like Qe5 and Rf3 just fending off his rook and queen, bleeding away most of a completely winning position. When your rook and bishop already have the enemy king trapped on the back rank, hunt for the forcing check sequence before anything quieter.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Qxc8 was sitting right there — your queen just takes the rook, and with your rook on e7 and bishop on f6 already boxing in Black's king, there's no clean way for him to get it back; the line even ends with Qf1+ Rxf1 and you're cruising. Qd5 lets that rook survive, and it costs you: Black's queen goes hunting through your pawns, taking a3, then d4, then h3, crawling right up next to your own king, until you need a move like R7e3 just to hold the position together. You were up nearly twenty pawns of evaluation — when you're that far ahead, grab the piece that's hanging instead of repositioning your queen somewhere quieter.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on f4 has been hanging to the pawn on g5 the whole time, and Bf5+ does nothing about it — you check, he blocks with e6, you retreat to c2, and gxf4 just wins that bishop for free, the same pattern that already burned you two moves earlier. The engine's idea is Nxg5 instead: after fxg5 Bxg5 you've only spent a knight for two pawns, but your bishop lands on g5 staring at e7 and d8, right where his king on d7 lives. That's the principle — with his king stuck in the center, look for ways to rip lines open, not spite checks that ignore your own loose pieces.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Notice your bishop on f4 sits right in front of the pawn on g5 — it's attacked, and Bf5+ ignores that completely. He plays e6 kicking your checking bishop, you retreat to c2, and gxf4 just wins the bishop outright since nothing defends f4. His king is still stuck on d7, uncastled, which is why the engine likes e4 instead: even after gxf4, exd5 rips the center open and hits the knight on c6, forcing Na7, then Qa4+ grabs more while his king is stranded. When the king's exposed like that, look for the move that opens lines against it, not a check that just drops material.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight was doing fine on e4, but Ng5 walks it straight into the only piece that can hit that square — his bishop on c1 has a totally clear diagonal down to g5, and nothing of yours defends it there. So Bxg5 just wins the knight for free, and the position swings from roughly equal to you being down a full piece. The safe square was d6: Nd6 tucks the knight back into your own camp, and even though he grabs the pawn with Rxe5+, you block with Be7, develop with Qe2 and Bg6, and you're only down a pawn instead of a piece. Before you send a piece forward, always check who's aiming at the square it's landing on.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: That knight on g5 is still hanging from last move — nothing defends it, and Be7 doesn't change that at all. He just plays Bxg5 and picks it up, compounding the loss instead of fixing it. The move you needed was Ne6, walking the knight back to safety on a square where it's actually useful — after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 you trade off his strong knight, and Bxd3 even grabs a pawn back, keeping the game roughly balanced. The lesson here is to always ask first: do any of my pieces currently hang? Only once that's answered should you look for your own ideas like developing the bishop.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: You were sitting comfortably at +0.8, but e4 lets a moment slip by. The sharper move was Bc7, dropping your bishop onto that square and hitting his queen on d8 directly — she has to move, say Qd7, and then you follow up with b6, cramping his queenside, and Ra4 lifting your rook into the game while his knight scrambles to c6 just to stay active. Playing e4 instead gives him a free tempo: he plays Bd7, finishing development on his own terms, and only then does Bc7 arrive — a move late, and far less effective. The habit to build: when a piece can hit the enemy queen with tempo, play that before anything slower.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: This one's about tempo. Qc5 right now hits the queen on b6, forcing Qd8, then Bd6 lands your bishop on a monster square eyeing e7 and f8, and after Re8 Bxe7 Rxe7 you've simplified into a clearly better structure. Qc3 does none of that — it's a passive square, so he gets a free tempo: Bd7, developing with a real threat on your undefended pawn on b5. By the time you try Qc5 a move later it's too late, Bxb5 just wins the pawn. Play the most forcing version of your idea immediately — a slower move first just hands the tempo away.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were already down badly, but Nb7 makes it worse by walking into a fork. His rook checks with Rc7+, your king goes to d8, and Rxb7 just scoops the undefended knight up for free. What you needed was Nf5+ — it checks his king on g3 and simultaneously attacks the rook on g7, so after Kf4 you simply play Nxg7, winning the rook back and turning a lost game into a real fight, following with Nh5 and c4. Before a knight move in a tight spot, scan whether it hits two things at once — that's exactly where your comeback chances live.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, +6.3, and Rd7 throws it all away in one move. Your rook lands on d7 with nothing defending it, and his rook on d1 is staring right down the same file — Rxd7 just wins your rook for free, and even after Bd6 trying to hit it back, bxc6 lets him grab your knight too. The move that was actually there was Bxg3+ — your bishop takes the pawn with check, forcing Kxg3, and then Rxd1 simply wins his rook since nothing guards it. That's the whole game right there: before you move a rook onto an open file, check what's already sitting on it, and always look for the forcing check first.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: The black king is trapped on e7 — your knight on f6 and its own pawns wall it in, and the queen on d8 is the only piece that can block a check on the 7th rank. Qxb7+ forces Qc7, and then Qxc7 isn't just winning the queen, it's mate — e7 has no square left to run to. Instead exd4 just nets a pawn and lets Bg7, dxc5, Rd7+ back in; you went from a mate-in-a-few position down to merely +8. When the king's only defender must block on one specific square, look for the check that turns that block into a mating net.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You had the right idea — Nd7 lands on a great fork square hitting the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — but the move order was backwards. Play Rd7+ first: the queen on c7 is forced to capture, Qxd7, and only then does Nxd7 recapture, landing on that same fork square while black has had zero time to save either piece. Play Nd7 directly like you did, and there's no check, so black just plays Bg7, tucking the bishop away before you can win it — you still keep a big edge, but you gave back nearly 4 pawns of advantage. Force the concession first, then jump into the fork.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your queen just stepped onto the same diagonal as his queen — e7, f6, g5, h4 — with nothing sitting on f6 or g5 to block it, so Qxh4 simply wins your queen for free. That's the whole story: no combination, no compensation, just a hanging piece on an open diagonal you didn't check before moving there. Qa3 instead tucks the queen onto a safe diagonal off the action, and after Re8, c4, d4, g4 you're the one making progress instead of bleeding material. Before you put your queen anywhere, scan every diagonal, file, and rank leading to it.

drills.explanation: Your e5 pawn was attacked by the d6 pawn; exd6 resolves it cleanly, and after cxd6 you develop normally with Nc3 and Nf3, dead level. Pushing e6 instead placed the pawn on a square Black's f7 pawn covers: fxe6 ate it for free, and after Bd3 Nf6 c4 you were simply a pawn down out of the opening.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: That e5 pawn doesn't threaten anything decisive on e6 — nobody defends it there, so f7 just scoops it up with fxe6 and you've handed back your space and material for nothing. exd6 instead cashes in properly: cxd6 recaptures, and then Nc3 followed by Ne5 gives you real central pressure while black's knight on d7 is still untangling. You had roughly a two-pawn edge from your development and space; e6 threw that away, exd6 keeps it working for you. Before pushing a pawn forward, check who actually defends the square it's landing on.

drills.explanation: Your queen on e5 was attacked by the knight on f3, and Qe6 was the safe square — it stays active and out of reach, and if Nd4 chases it again, Qe5 returns with White having nothing better than repeating. Qd6 stepped onto the open d-file instead: Rad1 hit the queen with your own rook on d8 lined up behind it, and after Qb4, Rxd8+ Bxd8 handed White the file and the initiative.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: Retreating to d6 hands White the open d-file — Rad1 doubles up against the rook you've left as its only defender, then Qb4 adds a second attacker on your bishop on e7, and you're forced into Rxd8+ Bxd8, trading down into a passive position. Qe6 instead keeps your queen centralized and flexible; after Nd4 Qe5 Nf3 you're just holding steady rather than surrendering the file. When your rook is the only piece guarding an open file, don't pull your queen away from it without checking what a rook lift like Rad1 does next.

drills.explanation: Bxb4 just takes a free pawn — the whole point of testing the Polish. White regains it with Bxe5, but after Nf6, c3, Be7 you've swapped his wing pawn for your e-pawn and developed smoothly. Nc6 guarded e5 but walked into b5: the knight had to retreat to e7, and Bxe5 took the pawn anyway — White kept his extra pawn and gained time.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: That b4 pawn is hanging the moment White plays it — nothing defends it, and your bishop on f8 can just take it, Bxb4, along the f8-b4 diagonal. Play Nc6 instead to guard e5, and White plays b5, kicking your knight to e7, then simply takes Bxe5 anyway — you never got the free pawn and still lost the one you were protecting. Bxb4 first grabs the pawn, and after Bxe5 Nf6 c3 Be7 d4 you're fully fine and developing normally. Don't spend a move defending something when the real prize is sitting undefended a diagonal away.

drills.explanation: Nd4 does everything at once: it saves the knight from the d5 pawn and attacks White's queen on f3, winning a free tempo. After Qd1 you follow with Bf5 and b5, developing with real energy. Nce7 retreated to a passive square that blocks your own f8 bishop, and gave White time for d4, building a big centre unchallenged.
drills.title: vs Aldr_in (958) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: When d5 kicks your knight on c6, retreating with Nce7 is passive — it just lets White play d4, grab more space, and develop with Ne2 while you're the one reacting. Nd4 actually punishes the pawn push: it jumps into the center attacking White's queen on f3, forcing Qd1 back, and after Bf5, d3, b5, c3 your knight sits beautifully centralized and you're setting the pace instead of following it. The principle: when a pawn attacks your piece, before retreating, check whether you can jump forward into a square that hits something of theirs — tempo beats a quiet retreat almost every time.

drills.explanation: Kb6 steps to safety, and play stays balanced: Rh5 Rg8, then Rxf5 for him and Rxg3 for you — an even pawn-grab. Kd6 walked onto exactly the square the knight on e5 forks from f7: Nf7+ hits king and rook together, and Ke7 Nxd8 Kxd8 costs you a rook for a knight. From e5, f7 was the springboard covering both d6 and d8.
drills.title: vs Aldr_in (958) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Your king on d6 and rook on d8 are both exactly a knight-hop from f7, and White's knight on e5 can reach that square with check — Nf7+ forks the two of them, and after Ke7, Nxd8, Kxd8 you've simply lost the rook for the knight. Kb6 avoids that fork square entirely and keeps the king safe while the rook stays connected; the game continues with Rh5, Rg8, and you're fighting on rather than down material. Before you move your king in an endgame with a knight still on the board, scan every square a knight's-move away from where you're headed.

drills.explanation: The e5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxe5 turns the threat around: it wins the pawn, and after Nxe5 Bxe5 your bishop sits beautifully in the center eyeing g7, leaving Black scrambling with Qg6 before you castle and meet Bf5 calmly. Castling first simply dropped the bishop — exf4 took it for free, and you were a piece down by move nine.
drills.title: vs dangalindo97 (884) — London System
drills.coachNote: Look at your bishop on f4 — Black's pawn on e5 attacks it directly, and it's only defended by the knight on c6 while you actually have two ways to hit e5 first. Castling with O-O ignores the hanging bishop completely, so exf4 just wins it outright; you get c4 and Re1+ for some activity, but you're a full piece down. The move was Nxe5: Nxe5, Nxe5, Bxe5 trades knights evenly and then your bishop scoops up the recapturing knight for free, since nothing else guards e5, leaving you up a clean pawn with a monster bishop staring at g7. Resolve a hanging piece before you spend a move on anything else — castling can wait.

drills.explanation: Qg4 stepped straight onto the c8-bishop's open diagonal — c8 to g4 had nothing in the way, and Bxg4 took the queen; after h3, Be6 the bishop went home and Black was simply up material. Qh5 was the safe square, or better yet Nd2 first: develop the stranded b1 knight, tuck the queen on e1, and Nf3 finally challenges the bishop on g5.
drills.title: vs dangalindo97 (884) — London System
drills.coachNote: Your queen jumping to g4 lands right on the c8-h3 diagonal, and Black's bishop is still on c8 with a totally clear path through d7, e6 and f5 — so Bxg4 just wins your queen for a bishop in a position that was already miserable. The idea, hitting the bishop on g5, was fine, but the square was wrong. Qh5 does the same job from safety: it attacks g5 directly, forces the bishop back to e7, and lets you fight on with Nd2 and eventually Rxf4 to win the f4 pawn back. Before you put a piece on a square, check every line running through it, not just what you're attacking from it.

drills.explanation: Both Black bishops were loose — f5 to your bishop on d3, g5 to your knight — but capture order decided everything. Bxf5 takes the one with a counter-capture available, since the f5 bishop and your d3 bishop attack each other; after gxf5, Nd4 centralizes powerfully. Nxg5 allowed the in-between move Bxd3, and after Qxd3 Qxg5 Black had won the piece right back.
drills.title: vs LeoAlayon (759) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Grabbing on g5 feels tempting, but two things are still unresolved: your bishop on d3 sits on the same diagonal as Black's bishop on f5, and the knight that just landed on g5 has nobody covering it. So Bxd3 comes first, you recapture Qxd3, and then Qxg5 simply picks off your knight for free — your 'winning' capture actually loses you a piece. Bxf5 was the fix: it removes the exact bishop pressuring d3, so nothing's left hanging, and after gxf5 Nd4 your position stays completely safe. When two of your pieces are under fire in the same position, deal with the one that's actually threatening you, not the one that's easiest to grab.

drills.explanation: Bxf5 resolves the bishop standoff your way: after Bxg5 Nxg5 Qxg5 you have Bd7 — the bishop lands in Black's camp hitting the knight on c6 and the rook on e8. dxe5 handed Black the move order: Bxg5 came first, and after Bxf5 gxf5 Nd4 the trades fizzled — about a pawn and a half lost purely to capturing in the wrong sequence.
drills.title: vs LeoAlayon (759) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Same story one move earlier — your bishop on d3 and Black's bishop on f5 are trading glares on that light diagonal, and your other bishop on g5 is only defended once, by the knight on f3. Snatching the e5 pawn ignores all that, so Black plays Bxg5 first; when you try to even it out with Bxf5, gxf5 just recaptures, and you've traded both your bishops for one of Black's plus a pawn. Bxf5 right away was the move: take the piece pressuring d3 before touching anything else, and after Bxg5 Nxg5 Qxg5 the trades come out clean instead of costing you material. Deal with the piece under attack before you go pawn-hunting.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a8 had the bishop on c8 pinned against the queen on d8, and Rfc1 — either rook works, but the f1 rook keeps a1 at home — piles onto it down the fully open c-file. Black's best is to bail out with Be6, when Qxd8+ Nxd8 trades into a pleasant endgame for you. g3 let the moment slip: d5 and then Nd6 covered c8, and the target wriggled free.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs hansk74 (917) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're crushing here, up over six pawns with your queen sitting deep on a8, but g3 does nothing to convert that — it just shuffles a kingside pawn while Black gets a free tempo to push d5 and reroute the knight to d6, clawing back some activity. Rfc1 was the real plan: it connects your rooks, and once Black plays Be6 you get Qxd8+, forcing a queen trade with Nxd8 exactly when you're up huge material — which is when you simplify, not complicate. From there d5 and Bxd5 mop it into a completely won ending. When you're this far ahead, every move should trade pieces or trade down the position, not just pass the turn.

drills.explanation: Nxe4 wins the e4 pawn cleanly — d5 can't recapture, because that would open the b3–g8 diagonal from your queen straight onto Black's king. After f5 the knight slides back to g3, and c4 starts prying at d5 next. Nh2 retreated for nothing: f5 cemented Black's pawn on e4, and you had to play f3 to challenge it anyway, a tempo and a pawn poorer.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs hansk74 (917) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Look at Black's pawn on e4 — it looks defended by the pawn on d5, but that d5 pawn is functionally pinned: your queen sits on b3, and the moment d5 disappears, the diagonal b3-c4-d5-e6-f7 opens straight onto Black's king on g8. So Nxe4 just wins the pawn clean, because Black can't actually recapture with dxe4 without dropping into Qb3+ — the engine has Black play f5 instead and just accept being down a pawn. Nh2 retreats your other knight and lets that moment pass; after f5 and Re8 the tension just dissolves and you never collect on e4. Before assuming a pawn is safely guarded, check whether its defender is actually free to move.
